nameStory: The white-tailed kite gets its name from its brilliant white tail feathers that flash like a beacon when it flies. Unlike many raptors with brown or dark tails, this bird's snowy white tail is so distinctive it became the defining feature in its common name.
description: The white-tailed kite is a small, elegant raptor about the size of a crow with striking black and white plumage. This graceful bird of prey has a white head, chest, and tail contrasting with pale gray wings marked by bold black shoulder patches. It's known for its unique hunting style of hovering motionless in mid-air like a feathered helicopter before diving down to catch prey.

idTips.label: White tail
idTips.description: Brilliant white tail feathers that appear almost luminous in flight, contrasting sharply with the gray wings and making the bird unmistakable even from a distance

idTips.label: Black shoulder patches
idTips.description: Bold black markings on the wing shoulders that look like dark epaulettes, visible both when perched and in flight against the pale gray wings

idTips.label: Hovering behavior
idTips.description: Distinctive hunting style of hanging motionless in the air with rapid wingbeats, often staying in one spot for 30 seconds or more before moving to a new position

idTips.label: White head and body
idTips.description: Clean white coloring on the head, chest, and belly with no streaking or barring, giving it an almost ethereal appearance in good light

idTips.label: Red eyes
idTips.description: Bright red to orange-red eyes that stand out against the white head, most visible when the bird is perched and you can get a close look

habitat: White-tailed kites are extremely rare visitors to New England, with only one recorded observation in the region. When they do appear, they favor open grasslands, agricultural fields, and marsh edges where they can hunt for small mammals. They prefer areas with scattered trees or poles for perching combined with expansive open ground for their distinctive hovering hunt.

seasonality.spring: Any white-tailed kite sighting would be extraordinary in spring. Look for the distinctive hovering behavior over open fields during migration periods.
seasonality.summer: Summer sightings would be exceptionally rare vagrant birds far from their normal western range. Hot weather might bring them to hunt over grasslands in early morning or evening.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration could theoretically bring a lost individual eastward, though this would be a once-in-a-lifetime sighting for most New England birders.
seasonality.winter: Winter appearances would be virtually impossible, as these birds don't tolerate cold climates and would likely move south if blown off course.

funFact: White-tailed kites can hover so precisely that they appear to be suspended by invisible strings, maintaining their position even in moderate winds by constantly adjusting their wing angle and tail position with computer-like precision.
confusionNotes: In New England, a white-tailed kite might be confused with a Northern Harrier, but harriers have longer, narrower wings and a white rump patch rather than a white tail. Remember: white TAIL for kite, white RUMP for harrier.
contextualKnowledge: White-tailed kites were once called 'White Kites' or 'Black-shouldered Kites,' and the population crashed in the early 1900s due to persecution and habitat loss before making a remarkable comeback. Any New England sighting would likely make local birding news and attract visitors from hundreds of miles away.
compareHints: As the only Elanus kite in North America, the white-tailed kite is most similar to other small raptors like the American Kestrel within the hawk family. However, kestrels have rusty-red backs and tails with distinct barring, while white-tailed kites have gray backs and pure white tails. Kestrels also have a more compact, chunky build compared to the kite's elegant, longer-winged silhouette.
